title: 🎩 Tech Monopolies Make Outages Worse | EFFector 38.21
content:
Service outages, like the ones we've seen take down everything from airlines to email, seem to be coming faster than ever. Their specific causes might be different, but these wide-scale service disruptions share one thing in common: the over-reliance on one company or system to make our world work. In our latest EFFector newsletter, we're talking about how digital monoculture has made tech companies too big to fail.

For over 35 years, EFFector has been your guide to understanding the intersection of technology, civil liberties, and the law. This issue covers ALPR at the ballot box, surveillance wearables, and how digital monoculture makes service outages worse.

Prefer to listen in? EFFector is now available on all major podcast platforms. This time we're talking to EFF's Rory Mir about tech monopolies, service outages, and what we can do to build a more resilient internet. You can find the episode and subscribe on your podcast platform of choice:

author: Rindala Alajaji
title: New York and California Age Gating Rules Go Into Effect in the New Year
content:
Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.

EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts. The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users.

Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976, which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709.

For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking.

At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives, meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors, while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users.

Along the same lines as the California regulations, New York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service.

As we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the New York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics.

The New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves, since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies "de-identify" age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)).

Echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in New York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives—meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week.

Under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today.

When young people lose accounts or get pushed into stripped-down experiences, they lose contact with friends, support groups, community organizing, local news, creative audiences, and ways to speak out on current issues. U.S. law has long recognized that people under 18 have their own constitutional rights to speak and receive information, and sweeping age gates directly interfere with those rights.

At the same time, lawmakers often sell age-verification mandates as a way to rein in Big Tech, yet the opposite happens in practice. Megacorporations like Meta and Google have the resources to build expensive age-estimation systems and absorb steep fines (such as $50,000 per violation in California) while they figure out compliance. Smaller platforms and independent communities such as Bluesky or Dreamwidth, however, cannot afford those legal risks or engineering costs. As we have already seen in states like Mississippi, crushing compliance burdens push smaller sites out of the market and drive users back toward the biggest corporate giants. Instead of holding Big Tech accountable, these rules entrench its dominance; leaving everyone with fewer community options, less innovation, and a more centralized surveillance machine.

Legislative and regulatory action are setbacks, but they do not settle the debate. If these rules affect you in California, New York, or anywhere else: keep a record while the details are still fresh, and share it with our team at agegates@eff.org.

Take screenshots and note the date, time, service, and what you were trying to do; write down what you lost (whether that means an account, a club or volunteer group, contact with friends, local news, or a favorite creator) or note if you chose to walk away from a service rather than submit an ID or personal data. You do not need to hand over sensitive information to show that these rules burdened you. If you hit an age check or parental-consent snag, save what the platform asked for, whether it worked or failed, any privacy promises or laws cited, and any appeal attempts.

If these restrictions get in your way, email EFF at agegates@eff.org and tell us what happened. Tracking real-world lockouts, age-check failures, and infringements on free speech puts us in a stronger position to challenge the worst of these restrictions in legislatures and the courts. At the same time, we will keep fighting for laws that actually make people safer online by curbing corporate surveillance and giving parents, youth, and all internet users meaningful choice and control.

author: Thorin Klosowski
title: Signal Moves to Block AI Agents
content:
Signal announced an update to its mobile apps on iOS and Android that seeks to curb issues with AI agents accessing private chats. This is a useful new barrier against a problem we’ve been highlighting this year in our Encrypt It Already campaign. And good news, it’s enabled by default so you don’t need to do anything except update the app.

Over the last year, both Google and Apple* have released AI features in their operating systems that can read the contents of apps. One of the ways it can do this is through screen analysis. Google calls this feature “Intelligent Screen Context,” while Apple refers to it as either “Onscreen Awareness” or “Visual Intelligence.”

Apple now provides a way to block Siri AI’s access to apps, but by default every app is available to Siri AI, so it’s up to the user to go in and put these guardrails up. Signal requests that protection on your behalf. Google doesn’t currently offer any sort of similar option. So Signal on Android does the best it can, by turning off screenshots when it detects an AI assistant attempting to access the screen. Signal’s solution helps ensure that, unless you go in and change the setting yourself, it defaults to the most private option.

author: Jacob Hoffman-Andrews
title: Outage Chaos: Who Turned Off All The Computer?
content:
It's been a tough couple of weeks for anyone trying to 

use email

, 

fly

, 

spend money

, 

use an Apple device

*, or do 

signals intelligence

. Technical service outages are nothing new, but why do so many big ones seem to be happening all at once? Are hackers, AI, and international conflicts to blame? And what can we do about it?




Since most service interruptions don't make the news, it's hard to get a baseline on how often we see them happen normally. But after a major incident like the 

Microsoft cloud outage on November 12

, any smaller disruption is more likely to become a story as part of a pattern instead of an isolated incident. We would have heard plenty about the 

Air Traffic Control problems

 anyway, but the November 18 disruption to the 

PlayStation Network

 might have gotten less attention. There might appear to be a spike or an upward trend in outages, but we can't easily verify that, and the increased coverage will tend to make it seem more significant and interconnected than it necessarily is regardless.




One boring reason we might see an uptick in problems right now is the date on the calendar. With Thanksgiving travel, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Giving Tuesday, and Surveillance Sunday (we assume) all coming up, organizations often schedule major system updates for the first three weeks of November. This helps them prepare for holiday traffic, and lets them shift the outage risk to the time before those dates when they may consider it far more important to maintain reliable service.




While none of these particular outages have yet been directly attributed to AI (

or to malicious hackers

), bank CEOs and the NSA briefed congress and 

reportedly attributed

 at least some of them to rushed attempts to patch vulnerabilities found by AI. That’s understandable: all software updates carry risk, and companies and governments are having to deploy more updates, and faster, than they’ve ever needed to before. Some of those updates are to important infrastructure, where an outage would be very disruptive, but the impact of leaving vulnerabilities unpatched would be even worse.




Vulnerabilities are a type of software bug that affects security. Once a vulnerability is found in a given piece of software and disclosed, typically the software maker will release a patch fixing that vulnerability. That’s why so many update notes say things like “performance improvements and security fixes” 

—

 the security fixes are patches to vulnerabilities.




Companies and governments that run infrastructure face a challenging tradeoff: deploy patches quickly or slowly and cautiously? Patching quickly is important to keep systems secure. But every software update runs a risk: any change to a deployed system can have unintended consequences that snowball into a disastrous outage.




This exacerbates a much deeper problem long discussed in the engineering culture of many, if not most organizations. Keeping networks, servers, and applications not just secure but resilient in the face of patches, reboots, and capacity changes requires an investment in staff, time, hardware, and processes for frequent maintenance, redundant systems, realistic staging environments, automated rollbacks, monitoring, and pre-deployment testing. These investments are rarely as attractive to decision

-

makers as a new product or feature, or at times, sadly, as layoffs.




This should come as no surprise when we think of our apps, web sites, airlines

,

 and bank cards as supported by electronic infrastructure. As in the more visible physical world, maintenance can only be deferred for so long before the costs become immediate and dramatic. We accept the cost of an occasional short term bridge closure to reduce the risk of a bridge collapse, and highway departments schedule road work nearly every night of the year to repair and prevent the worst potholes.




When this kind of work is endlessly deferred in the world of software, we speak of 

technical

 debt

: 

issues we already know about that aren't causing a big enough problem right now to divert us from other work, but that, if left unaddressed, can easily multiply and interact to cause outages or other complications

.

 This can show up as routine steps that have to be done by hand instead of automatically on a schedule, a programmer's shortcut that works well in one specific situation but is more fragile in general, an operating system six months (or years) overdue for a reboot, or a piece of networking hardware no longer supported for patches by its manufacturer. On the other hand, when maintenance work is well-resourced and routine, it should be rare for even major security updates to cause significant issues.




What’s needed in the short term is a big investment in the people and training needed to roll out patches promptly and safely. What’s needed in the long term is a big investment in software security, eliminating entire classes of vulnerabilities, like memory safety, before they are ever written.




For organizations that have gotten used to patching slowly and cautiously, suddenly switching gears to patching quickly is a big challenge. And the 

flood of vulnerability disclosures enabled by AI

 means that everyone is being asked to switch gears like that at once.




Fortunately, it’s not a zero-sum game: patches can be rolled out quickly and cautiously, with investments in reducing technical debt and expanding maintenance budgets as described above. These measures are expensive and time-consuming, but necessary. For governments asking how to respond to AI-enabled cybersecurity threats, investing in the people and training necessary to stay on top of patches will pay big dividends in reliability and security.




For individuals, consider the trade-offs when relying on a single provider for many services you rely on. Consumer cloud and device offerings tie together many of the things we need to function on a daily basis like email, messaging, file storage, and even payments, but that convenience and simplicity comes with the risk of losing access to it all if that service goes offline (or 

suspends your account

). Trying out 

interoperable alternatives

 is a great way to reduce your reliance on a single company.




Finally, for any critical data, learn the 3-2-1 rule for backups: Keep three different copies on two different types of storage with one copy in a different physical location. For many users, a laptop or other personal device, cloud storage, and a local backup disk exemplify this rule, as long as the laptop stores data on its own drives, not only in the cloud.




Among other things, the accelerated rollout of AI has made it all the more critical  to reinvest in people and systems to keep our software, networks, governments, and interconnected world stable.

author: Rory Mir
title: Outage Chaos: When Tech is too Big to Fail
content:
Outages happen, but we deserve a resilient internet where no one outage at one company can put people at risk and disrupt the global economy. We can only get there by addressing an over-reliance on a few cloud monopolists through effective antitrust laws and interoperability requirements.

Service outages, like we’ve seen recently at Microsoft, Apple*, banks, courts, airlines, and elsewhere, can be more than an annoying hurdle. Losing a vital service due to an error can cause the same impacts as a government-ordered internet shutdown—people losing access to vital information and lines of communication. As usual, the greatest harms are faced by people on the margins globally.

There’s not much hope in companies out-nerding these issues either. Technical errors will always exist, whether it’s a bug, negligence from an administrator, or a malicious attack. The problem is an over-reliance on any one company or system when these inevitable outages occur. It’s a matter of public safety and economic stability that policymakers mitigate the impact of these disruptions before they occur.

In order to do so, we must ensure antitrust prevents providers of key technical systems from becoming too big to fail.

The harms inflicted by tech monopolies go beyond monetary costs to the end user. In fact, monopolists can often offer lower prices, or even offer free services, thanks to their greater scale and incentive to shut out competitors using free-flowing investment capital. The problem is this puts a few tech companies in a position of incredible influence. The true cost is a loss of control when our private data, access to knowledge, and free expression all become mediated by tools owned by a handful of billionaires.

Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone.

This isn’t just a bad deal for us as individuals. Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone. When everything from daily tasks to national security is reliant on a few digital monocultures, one mistake or exploit can cascade into an explosive impact. The risks multiply in the current investment climate, where financial markets reward companies that strip-mine redundancy and resiliency from critical systems. Even if you see the problem coming, an outage that hits clients, suppliers, collaborators or loved ones proves just as disruptive. We need to remove these chokepoints for good, which means a digital sovereignty movement that makes the web more free by design—not just importing existing levers of control into another nation's borders.

Central to this effort must be undercutting platform control by fostering interoperability, i.e. when tools are made to be compatible among competitors. When this is done carefully, it’s not only easier to switch to better alternatives, we wind up with more alternatives as it becomes more viable to compete or offer complementary tools alongside existing systems.

This is what made systems like email great. You could choose your own apps and services, even using several simultaneously, and never lose touch with a contact. Early architects of the internet did not take reliable hosting for granted. Services were often on a machine a few rooms over, and needed to be prepared for the occasional interruption of service.

But in the age of hyperscalers and massive data centers, the infrastructure underlying the web isn’t owned by many scattered IT departments, it’s rented from a handful of “cloud” providers. These providers managed to scale up quickly and replace interoperability with walled gardens, enticing customers with lower costs while making it costly to leave and tightly controlling how services behave. Once in control, these platforms have every incentive to enshittify their services and devalue their workers, delivering an increasingly shoddy and restrictive service.

This context makes building interoperability an act of defiance—often coming from the sweat of open source developers. These projects may be tolerated by monopolists in the short term, but can be one boardroom decision away from being broken entirely. A better internet means championing these creators through funding, liability protections, and requiring big players to cooperate. Here is what lawmakers should do:

Federal and state legislators should—

Defend competitive compatibility. Developers merely providing alternative interfaces for tools should be shielded from liability. In the U.S., that means explicit protections under DMCA, CFAA, and corporate Terms of Service agreements. These protections should cover shared protocols and APIs as well as automated content retrieval through scraping.

Encourage interoperability. Lawmakers should force open key aspects of platform infrastructure by requiring big tech to support: (1) data portability, so users can move to a new service (2) back-end interoperability, to support more tools with competitive compatibility and (3) delegability, so people are not prevented from having code act on their behalf. So far, the Digital Markets Act in the EU has provided some positive examples of such legislation

Fund open source. In order to be sustainable, interoperable tools and standards cannot rely solely on corporate interest and volunteer labor. Programs like the EU Sovereign Tech Fund could help create viable alternatives within and beyond the borders of the EU.

Municipalities and institutions should—

Buy interoperable services. At any level, government agencies should set minimum interoperability requirements in procurement and hold a competitive bidding process to evaluate vendors’ privacy, security and lock-in risks. Agencies dependent on a sole provider, including through cooperative purchase agreements, are stuck with corporate price-gouging and even higher switching costs.

Fund Departments of Information Technology. Cloud services are often adopted to offset spending on IT professionals but, when these departments atrophy, institutions become even more reliant on the cloud providers. Maintaining in-house talent prevents this cycle of dependency and improves emergency responses to outages.

Adopt a plus-one approach to public communications. Institutions shouldn’t force citizens into walled gardens just to access public communications. In addition to posts to corporate social media, government agencies should share the same information on an open protocol—whether it’s bluesky, the fediverse, or just an RSS feed. By putting these in the open, more people will have access to urgent alerts and can create new useful tools.

Building a more resilient and democratic internet is possible, and many people are already hard at work doing just that. Above are some necessary steps to get corporate and government interests out of the way of rewilding the net with greater community and individual controls. The dream of the internet as a digital commons operating for the public good is not dead yet, and is worth fighting for.

*Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

author: Guest Author
title: Surveillance Isn't Safety: A Comic About Organizing Against Flock and Other Foes
content:
In the new comic "Surveillance Isn't Safety"—available for free today— cartoonist Bryn Adams explores the growing movement against mass surveillance through their involvement in the community fight against Flock Safety in Cleveland, Ohio. It's a personal journey that will resonate widely with residents in hundreds of cities where communities are drawing the line against automated license plate readers (ALPRs).

Published in collaboration between EFF and Crucial Comix, Bryn's comic captures the authenticity of the grassroot backlash against the surveillance industry—undercutting Flock founder Garrett Langley's latest dubious defense that public opposition of his company's product isn't real.

At the International Association of Chiefs of Police conference this fall, Langley accused the anti-surveillance activism of being driven by Russian bots and as being "inorganic." He pointed to the fact that many local groups were using similar language in their protest signs as supposed proof, when in reality, shared slogans are one of the hallmarks of a social movement. This was all misdirection from the grim realities that Flock and other ALPR systems facilitate: the mistakes are real; the abuse is real; the racism is real; and the targeting of dissenters, migrants, and abortion seekers is real. And, importantly, the cancelled contracts are real.

Bryn's comic sheds light on the real abuses and threats driving communities to mobilize against Flock, Axon, and other ALPR vendors. It shows that coast-to-coast activism doesn't happen overnight—any more than a comic appears out of thin air as a finished product. As advisors on the cartoon, EFF watched how Bryn's script evolved from rough sketches to penciled drawings, then to inked and shaded panels, mirroring how the long-running movement against mass surveillance has steadily snowballed over the last few years.

There is nothing “inorganic” about either: Both are built on passion, commitment, and putting in the work.

author: Joe Mullin
title: The Justice Department Wants To Give Patent Trolls More Power
content:
Software patents are mostly vague, hard to define, and widely abused. Most tech patent lawsuits aren’t filed by companies that make real products. They’re filed by patent trolls, companies that acquire patents to extract payments through litigation and legal threats.

A patent on one feature of a smartphone shouldn’t give the patent owner the power to threaten the existence of the entire product line. But that is exactly the leverage patent trolls want—and the current administration is helping them to get it.

In two recent patent cases, Radian Memory Systems v. Samsung and Collision Communications v. Samsung, the Justice Department and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office have asked courts to make it easier for patent owners to get injunctions. These are judicial orders that can force companies to stop selling products or remove features from them, rather than simply pay monetary damages.

The threat of an injunction can pressure a company to pay far more than what a patent is actually worth. In 2006, NTP Inc., a patent holding company with no products of its own, was able to pressure BlackBerry manufacturer Research in Motion Ltd. to pay a $612 million settlement when it was on the verge of an injunction.

In May 2006, the Supreme Court rejected the practice of granting permanent injunctions almost automatically after a finding of patent infringement. In eBay v. MercExchange, the high court held that patent owners must satisfy the same tough requirements that plaintiffs in non-patent cases must meet to get a permanent injunction. After eBay, patent owners had to show “irreparable harm,” that they can’t be adequately compensated by money, that the “balance of hardships” favors the plaintiff, and, critically, that an injunction would not harm the “public interest.”

At EFF, we celebrated eBay v. MercExchange as a major win for internet users. More than twenty years ago, we saw that software patents were going to be a disaster—not just for small companies (which they are), but for freedom of expression online. As EFF explained in its brief:

The United States Patent and Trademark Office has issued patents on methods fordownloading video programs, publishing web pages, sending email messages, making internet telephone calls, and even online fundraising methods. Injunctions against uses of these technologies—and many similar technologies—will inevitably affect, and may even chill, free expression on the internet.

The eBay rules make sense because the monopolies provided by patents are only justified when they serve a public purpose: promoting scientific and technological progress. Enforcing patents is not supposed to come at the cost of later innovators, free expression, or people’s access to technology.

Now, two decades after eBay, the government is urging courts to interpret those protections in ways that could give patent owners greater leverage. It’s unusual for the government to intervene in private patent disputes, but the current administration has done so repeatedly—and not on the side of the public.

In June 2025, the Justice Department and Patent Office filed a “statement of interest” in Radian Memory Systems v. Samsung, a dispute over patents involving solid-state drives (SSDs), the storage devices commonly used in modern computers. Radian, a patent assertion company tied to Fortress Investment Group, sought a preliminary injunction that would block sales of Samsung’s products even before a judge or jury had decided whether there was patent infringement.

In its statement, the government argued that even a patent owner whose business depends entirely on patent licensing could suffer irreparable harm, because calculating how much money it should get might be difficult. “In cases of unique assets, courts have commonly found irreparable harm when damages are difficult to calculate,” the DOJ writes in its brief.

But courts regularly resolve disagreements about patent royalty rates, a patent’s contribution, and comparable licenses. The fact that those disagreements exist does not, by itself, establish that monetary damages wouldn’t be enough to compensate the patent owner. If courts adopted the DOJ’s views here, a difficult but ordinary part of patent litigation could become a reason for finding irreparable harm, making it easier for patent owners to seek injunctions that threaten entire product lines. Pure patent-licensing businesses would love that—they would routinely start to ask for injunctions, since eBay’s most important protections would be weakened.

The government also says that “the prospect of an injunction can facilitate negotiation among the parties.” That’s exactly the problem. A company negotiating under threat of shutdown might pay massive sums to patent litigation shops in order to avoid disruption to product lines or customers. The payment is more likely to reflect the value of the threat, rather than the value of a patent. Radian ultimately withdrew its request for a preliminary injunction, but the government's arguments about when injunctions should be available remain concerning.

Remarkably, the government returned to this argument in February of this year, in a case called Collision Communications v. Samsung, which had already gone to trial. In this case, Collision, a patent-licensing entity that acquired its patents from a defense contractor, was awarded a $445.5 million jury verdict for infringement of four patents, and then sought an injunction.

Even though the jury had awarded Collision $445.5 million in damages, the government still intervened in the case, arguing that patent owners like Collision, which do not make products, should not be denied injunctions because they rely on patent licensing. They also argued that the difficulty of calculating monetary damages can support an injunction.

Although the court agreed that Collision had suffered irreparable harm and that monetary damages would be inadequate, U.S. District Court Judge Rodney Gilstrap rejected Collision’s argument that ongoing patent infringement automatically establishes irreparable harm. He ultimately denied the injunction because Collision didn’t satisfy two other requirements of the eBay test: showing that the balance of hardships favored an injunction and that an injunction would not harm the public interest.

Now Collision has appealed, and the argument is in front of the Federal Circuit, the nation’s top patent court. A brief from the Public Interest Patent Law Institute (PIPLI) explains what is at stake: when a patent owner doesn’t have any products, an injunction can prevent the public from accessing critical technology altogether. Since the patents here involve how mobile phones connect to cellular networks, “the effect on the public goes far beyond what these patents claim as improvements,” PIPLI explains.

The outcome could extend well beyond these two companies. The eBay test requires courts to consider who a permanent injunction would hurt, and who would benefit—including the public. A patent owner’s desire for more negotiating leverage should not override the interests of millions of people who rely on their phones. Yet that’s exactly the kind of leverage the government’s arguments could make it easier for patent owners to obtain, at the expense of the public.

Patent owners can already collect damages and royalties when their patents are infringed. But they should not get a shortcut to shutting down tech products just because calculating damages is hard work.

The Justice Department should defend the eBay safeguard. Instead, this administration is helping patent owners find ways around it. Courts should reject those arguments. We shouldn’t even have to say it, but we do: making patent threats more valuable does not align with the public’s interest.

This post is the second of a three-part series about how the current administration is using its power to give patent holders more power at the public’s expense. The final post will publish next week. See our previous post:

How the USPTO is undermining patent reviews

title: The Paramount-Warner Brothers Deal Could Usher in Another Age of Lost Media
content:
There are all sorts of reasons to be against the merger of Paramount and Warner Brothers-Discovery. There's the obvious problem of increasing concentration in the already pretty-concentrated film and TV industry. People have problems with Paramount's owner Skydance interfering with its news coverage and late night comedy. But one of the biggest is the way we are losing choice and access to information and culture.

In the context of the digital world, there are two major problems with these mega mergers. One, as we've said in the past, is that it further degrades the already awful state of mainstream streaming services. In short, by increasing the amount of legacy content under their control, major studios don't have to invest in either new content or well-engineered services to get users. author: Josh Richman
title: Privacy's Defenders Podcast: Snowden Exposes NSA’s Lies
content:
By 2013, EFF had spent seven years arguing in court that the National Security Agency was sweeping up ordinary Americans’ communications, including through the secret room that whistleblower Mark Klein had exposed. The government would neither confirm nor deny it, and outside the courtroom the public seemed to have moved on.

Then, in early June, documentary filmmaker Laura Poitras and journalist Glenn Greenwald mysteriously missed a Freedom of the Press Foundation board meeting at EFF’s offices. It turned out they were in Hong Kong, meeting an NSA contractor who had been secretly writing to Laura for months. His name was Edward Snowden, he had thousands of secret documents proving the government had in fact been spying on millions of Americans. When he subsequently revealed himself, a photo of him sitting behind his laptop – emblazoned with a big red EFF sticker – went worldwide.

(You can also find this episode on the Internet Archive and on YouTube.)

author: Victoria Python
title: EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework
content:
The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches.




Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred.




While the White House and leaders of major AI companies have claimed that no action is necessary, understandably, lawmakers at all levels and of both parties are proposing legislation to create new, additional safety protocols. These incidents may warrant legislative action. However, the good news is that post-incident reports indicate 

new

 protocols are largely unnecessary. Following 

existing

 best practices would have been enough to prevent the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and others like it. In other words, responsible AI developers can take immediate action to protect the public by implementing well-established security precautions as they develop and test their systems.




Lawmakers should start by referencing existing legal protections, including claims like negligence, gross negligence, trespass to chattels, Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), and computer trespass statutes like the Consumer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and analogous state law provisions, such as Section 502 of the California Penal Code.




Policymakers can help protect the public by requiring AI developers to follow established security protocols—and creating legal liability for failing to do so. These policies would protect the public from irresponsible actions by AI developers without impeding innovation. To the extent that gaps in existing laws warrant new legislation, EFF recommends the following policy framework:







STATUTORY SECURITY REQUIREMENTS: 

Lawmakers should enact legislation that requires AI developers to adhere to well-established cybersecurity best practices when testing AI systems, such as strong sandboxing and network isolation, least-privilege access, effective logging and monitoring, and clear incident-response procedures




REGULATORY STANDARDS: 

Congress should require an existing federal agency, such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

1

, to adopt safety standards for pre-deployment development and testing of generative AI systems, based on the established best practices referenced above. The agency should be required to update the standards every 2 years, or earlier as needed due to reported security incidents and/or major technological advancements. These standards should be developed in consultation with academic and nonprofit AI researchers, civil liberties organizations, and commercial AI developers, and adopted through formal agency rulemaking following a notice and comment process. That consultation should include an assessment of potential adverse impacts on competition, with the goal of ensuring that regulatory standards do not effectively lock out potential competitors.




LIABILITY: 

The law should provide for civil liability for AI development and testing that results in unauthorized access to a third party system, if performed under conditions that do not satisfy cybersecurity standards adopted by NIST, or another federal agency responsible for adopting these regulations, unless the company proves it acted reasonably under the circumstances to prevent unauthorized access to third party system 




ENFORCEMENT: 

Both federal and state authorities should be able to hold AI developers accountable where they have failed to meet the minimum standards adopted by the designated federal agency, such as NIST. Providing for state—in addition to federal—enforcement power reduces the risk of regulatory capture. Regulators should require independent investigations and notification of affected parties in the event of a security incident involving unauthorized access to a third party’s computer system. Finally, legislation should include an appropriately targeted private right of action.







The public shouldn’t have to worry about the risks of reckless AI development—or give up the benefits of AI just to prevent irresponsible developers from causing harm. By adopting policies that address demonstrated risks, lawmakers can provide meaningful public protection without hampering the development of useful tools.




1

NIST, the NSA, and CISA have recently issued a set of 

voluntary practices

 for managing security incidents during the training and evaluation of AI agents. Those practices may inform but do not substitute for the regulatory standards that should be developed according to the public, participatory process outlined here.

author: Thorin Klosowski
title: Tech Companies Are Trying to Shift the Entire Concept of Privacy (Again)
content:
Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did.

Meta and Google’s smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s* Audio Intelligence feature turns every Apple Watch into a transcription machine that records or summarizes your day. Amazon’s Bee devices take that a step further and can record and transcribe everything. Dozens of other companies are introducing pendants, rings, and other products designed to record, transcribe, or summarize everything we say and do all day long.

Privacy has always been a team sport. The actions you take with communication apps, collaborative software, or your cloud backup solutions, have long impacted everyone else you’re interacting with. But moving those choices deeper into the physical world where strangers, colleagues, family, and friends are all now a part of your privacy choices is drastically changing the game.

Tech companies want us to accept a reality where one person’s privacy choices (or lack thereof) means you suddenly need to be an expert in consumer tech who understands the capabilities of many devices on the market, how they work, how and if they signal when they’re recording, and what platforms they do or do not connect to. They believe these ambient surveillance devices that work in the background and are designed to look as normal as possible are the future, while they also expect the owners of these devices to use them responsibly and to notify those around them of their capabilities to act within whatever laws their states may have.

This is not reasonable, nor how consent works in any practical sense.

Let’s break this down by looking at some of the biggest players currently in the game: Apple and Amazon, who have two different takes on transcribing audio throughout the day, as well as Meta and Google, who both have slapped AI and cameras onto eyeglasses.

Ask Apple about privacy concerns and they’ll point to a white paper that explains all the technical barriers between them as a company and the data generated by the watch. Ask Meta and they’ll talk about all the ways you can customize the privacy controls or how certain details, like faces, may be blurred out when you interact with Meta AI through the glasses (but not during standard recording). Google does this too. Amazon will also talk about how you’re always in control, and no audio is stored (though it’ll also let you enable Amazon store integration, so your conversations can directly result in ads for products). And so on across all the companies making these products.

Some of these solutions do a better job than others at cutting out potential law enforcement or company access to this data. There will be a time to dive into these details more deeply, but the technical privacy promises these companies focus on only cover the consumer and user of the device. They ignore every bystander you interact with and their inability to actually opt out. There is no technical protection for you as a non-user of these devices, the person who finds yourself captured by them.

Still, we hope to look deeper into the technical differences between this category of devices soon.

With something like Apple’s Audio Intelligence and Amazon’s Bee devices, it may be best to treat them similar to an always-recording microphone, even if companies try to claim there’s “technically” no audio recording. These tools still often use a microphone to capture raw audio from conversations and convert it into summaries or transcripts before discarding the audio. Google's blog post notes that it has whole responsible use part of their Terms of Service where users have to agree not to record others without permission or in sensitive places.

But it’s not just the question of the legality from the point of view of the user. Law enforcement will eventually try to compel access to the data that these products create (either real-time audio or the summaries and transcripts they create). And while some products, like Apple’s Audio Intelligence, are engineered to make that difficult, not every product will be. We know from history that when data exists, governments will do everything they can to access it. There’s no reason to think something would change today.

There is a problem humming along in the background that is impossible to address with technical or legal solutions. If secretly documenting conversations becomes the norm, it makes every private conversation less spontaneous and open. It breaks a longstanding social norm that you will not record and document every conversation with friends, family, colleagues, or strangers.

The companies that make these sorts of products like to claim they’re no different from tools we already have. You can easily record everything right now with a phone or a camera. Heck, you can do so with a camcorder or cassette recorder if you want. And you can transcribe conversations with pen and paper, too. But those are actionable steps we take that both require effort from the user, and are clear to others around us. This new wave of passive surveillance tech is designed to encourage continuous monitoring and hide its use.

Even taken at face value, none of these products can understand the complex social context we all navigate every day. We intrinsically know there are different social agreements we all make when we’re standing on a street corner, at a protest, in a bathroom, at a doctor’s office, at the gym, or in a restaurant. Taking notes in a meeting at work is completely normal. Getting a summary of a conversation with your best friend about their divorce is not. Always-on monitoring of our conversations is an unacceptable burden on our conversational privacy.

Google seems to all but admit this problem in a conversation with CNN when it described the company’s experiments with a notification system that would alert people’s phones when someone was recording nearby:

“And just alerting bystanders doesn’t do much to help, [Juston Payne, senior director of product management at Google] said. “It can actually be weirdly disempowering to you in that you’re like, ‘What am I meant to do now?’” he said.”

It’s easy to buy into the tech company line that these products are inevitable, but we’ve seen so many vaporware products over the years that we should take those claims of success with a grain of salt. We’ve seen entire product categories come and go within just a few years, and if the public doesn’t want this stuff, the tech companies will have to throw in the towel.

Of course, that doesn’t mean we all just have to sit around and hope that’s what happens. For its part, Apple launched its Audio Intelligence features in beta specifically to get feedback, and we think it’s worth taking the time to fill out their feedback forms (or in the Feedback Assistant app if you’re in the beta) and let them know what you think.

Products from the likes of Meta, Google, Amazon, and others might be harder to push back on, but politely and clearly engaging with those who use them in ways that make you uncomfortable is a good place to start. And if you see abusive videos on social networks where these sorts of products are used, report them. If you find these products useful for yourself, make it clear to those around you when you’re using them, and only do so with consent and in social moments where it makes sense to do so.

*Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

title: We’re Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches
content:
Today, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant, a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.

Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. author: Joe Mullin
title: Why Fewer People Are Challenging Bad Patents
content:
The number of petitions being filed at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) has collapsed. That’s not reason for celebration. The PTAB is an important line of defense against low-quality software patents being used in lawsuits against people and companies.

The drop didn’t happen because suddenly patents have become higher quality. It’s simply because USPTO leadership is increasingly refusing to consider good challenges to patents, for reasons unrelated to the merits. The process has become so unreliable that many would-be patent challengers aren’t even trying.

Inter partes review (IPR) is a process that allows people to challenge patents at the Patent Office, rather than having to fight an expensive lawsuit in federal court. It’s one of the most important ways to get bad patents out of the system.

In the third quarter of 2026, July through September, only 97 IPR petitions were filed at the PTAB, compared to 327 petitions during the same period in 2025. Similarly, only 37 IPR petitions were filed in September 2026, compared to 129 petitions in December 2024—the last full month before the current USPTO leadership began reshaping how the Board handles patent challenges.

author: Sophia Cope
title: U.S. Supreme Court Deals Final Blow to Corporate Human Rights Accountability
content:
For the past two decades, the U.S. Supreme Court has been slowly weakening the Alien Tort Statute (ATS), a key human rights law that allows foreign nationals to sue persons or entities in civil court for harms resulting from violations of international law. The court’s recent ruling in Cisco Systems, Inc. v. Doe I dealt the law a final blow, foreclosing—absent new legislation by Congress—any future ability by plaintiffs to use the law to hold technology companies accountable for aiding and abetting human rights abuses. EFF filed multiple amicus briefs in the case, including most recently in the Supreme Court.

The ATS was passed by the very first Congress in 1789 and in just a few words gives U.S. federal courts jurisdiction to hear civil claims brought by foreign nationals against defendants who violated “the law of nations or a treaty of the United States." There has been a longstanding question about what counts as a valid civil claim under “the law of nations.”

In Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain (2004), the Supreme Court had noted three historical international law claims that the First Congress likely had in mind: violation of safe conducts, infringement of the rights of ambassadors, and piracy, collectively known as the Blackstone Three.

title: Google Summaries Aren't About AI, They're About Lock-In
content:
Whether they call it AI summaries, knowledge panels, or AMP, Google takes actions that are less about functionality and more about locking you into its own ecosystem. Knowing that makes it possible for all of us to choose better services than Google's, defeating their anticompetitive goal. In this case, as it is so often, knowledge is power. 

 




In the old days, when dinosaurs roamed the earth and getting online involved your computer making eldritch shrieking, Google was a website that took whatever you typed in and gave you a list of links that best matched what you were searching for. title: Postal Service Surveilled Protest Activities Online With Little Rules, Oversight
content:
The U.S. Postal Service used social media surveillance to monitor and report on protests across the political spectrum, government records show.

The records, disclosed to EFF and other requesters suing the postal service under the Freedom of Information Act, show that the agency’s internet Covert Operations Program, or iCOP, routinely sifted through social media posts organizing and discussing protests with little records of any oversight or legal justification.

EFF filed suit in 2021 after Yahoo News disclosed the program’s existence and how the agency used it to monitor First Amendment protected activities. They included a planned “Million MAGA March,” a guns rights advocacy event and counter-protest in Virginia, a nationwide Save the Post Office Saturday protest, and planned protests in front of then-Postmaster General Louis DeJoy’s home in Washington, D.C.

content:

title: Why VPNs Are Worth Defending
content:
Developers of virtual private network (VPN) apps are reporting that their products are again being pulled from Apple’s App Store in Russia. This is an unacceptable crackdown on a vital tool to protect privacy and speech online.

Why? VPNs give people a way to control their own online activities. When you visit a website through a VPN, that website only sees the VPN server's location (well, IP address) rather than your actual location. It's like sending a letter through a P.O. box so the recipient doesn't know where you really live. It can also disguise where you’re accessing information from, which can make it possible to access information banned by your government.

This is an unacceptable crackdown on a vital tool to protect privacy and speech online.

Going after tools that give people the space to communicate and access information freely is a common tactic from the totalitarian playbook. This latest demand comes after several steps the Russian government’s taken to surveil speech specifically on Apple products. In 2024, the Moscow Times reported that Russia’s state media watchdog, Roskomnadzor, went after VPN apps on the Apple App Store, after banning access to Western social media platforms and blacklisting opposition media sites. Russia then blocked Apple’s FaceTime software in 2025, according to Apple Insider.
